text: A classical bit sitting in memory doesn't care how long you wait before reading it. A qubit does care — the moment it's created, it starts leaking quantum information into its environment, and that leak is the single biggest reason quantum computers need error correction at all.

A physical qubit holds an arbitrary superposition, alpha ket-zero plus beta ket-one, and that superposition is the whole point — it's what lets quantum algorithms explore many possibilities at once. But it only exists as long as the qubit stays isolated, and no real qubit ever fully is: it sits in a dilution refrigerator next to control wiring, bathed in stray electromagnetic fields, weakly coupled to everything nearby. Decoherence is what happens when that coupling lets quantum information leak out a tiny bit at a time — the environment effectively measures the qubit without anyone intending it, and enough of those tiny measurements collapse the superposition into something close to a classical, definite 0 or 1.

Every qubit has two decoherence clocks. T1, the energy relaxation time, is how long a qubit prepared in the excited state 1 takes to decay back to the ground state 0 by losing energy — typically tens to hundreds of microseconds for today's superconducting qubits, and usually the headline number quoted for a technology. T2, the dephasing time, is subtler: it's how long a superposition keeps the correct relative phase between its 0 and 1 components, even if no energy is lost at all. T2 is always less than or equal to twice T1, and in practice it's often the more restrictive limit on how long a superposition stays useful.

Here's what that looks like as a number. Treating decoherence as simple exponential decay, the probability a qubit has decohered by the time a gate finishes is 1 minus e to the minus t over T1. Using an illustrative T1 of 100 microseconds: a 20-nanosecond gate carries about a 0.02% chance of decohering, 50 nanoseconds about 0.05%, 200 nanoseconds about 0.2%, and a full microsecond about 1%. For gate times much shorter than T1, the risk scales almost linearly with time — double the duration, double the risk.

That's why today's quantum processors are called NISQ devices — Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum — and the 'noisy' isn't a hedge, it's the central engineering fact of this era. Decoherence can't be engineered away to zero with physical qubits alone, and those individually tiny per-gate probabilities compound fast: chain together the hundreds or thousands of gates a real algorithm needs, and a near-certainty of at least one error appears somewhere in the circuit. That compounding is exactly the open problem the rest of this course exists to solve.
Next lesson: the two fundamental error types, bit-flip and phase-flip, that every quantum error-correcting code in this course is built from the ground up to catch.
